s: The book's answer: a capitalist (mixed) system is in practice in Pakistan, although the aim is an Islamic economic system.
mcqs.n: Pakistan's economy is often described as a mixed economy with mostly capitalist features.

mcqs: In socialism the government (central planning authority) makes the basic economic decisions.
Wealth in Pakistan is unequally distributed.
In an interest-free economy investment is encouraged through profit-sharing, so employment opportunities increase.
Profit-and-loss sharing (PLS) accounts began in Pakistan in 1981.
In socialism the means of production are under collective (state) ownership.
Islam recognises natural differences in ability and means (natural equality), not absolute equality.
The capitalist system supports free trade and free markets.
Interest has a central position in the capitalist system.
Karl Marx presented the concept of the socialist economic system (Das Kapital).
The WTO came into being on 1 January 1995.
Partnership in profit and loss (mudarabah, musharakah) is a feature of the Islamic economic system.
longQuestions: Capitalism is an economic system in which the means of production are privately owned and economic activities are guided by the price mechanism and the profit motive.

Characteristics: (1) Right of private property; (2) Freedom of enterprise — anyone may start any business; (3) Profit motive; (4) Price mechanism — demand and supply decide what, how and for whom to produce; (5) Competition among producers and sellers; (6) Consumer's sovereignty.

(7) Freedom of choice of occupation and consumption; (8) Right of inheritance; (9) Minimum government interference (laissez-faire); (10) Interest-based banking and credit; (11) Inequality of income; (12) Saving and investment by private individuals; (13) Free trade.

(1) Unequal distribution of wealth — the rich become richer and the poor poorer; (2) Exploitation of workers by capitalists — low wages and long hours; (3) Monopolies harm consumers by high prices; (4) Trade cycles — booms and depressions cause unemployment.

(5) Wastage of resources through competition and advertising; (6) Production of luxuries for the rich instead of necessities for the poor; (7) Interest system — concentration of wealth and exploitation; (8) Class conflict between workers and owners; (9) Neglect of social welfare.
(10) Materialism — moral values are ignored for profit; (11) Consumer's sovereignty is limited by low incomes; (12) Hoarding, speculation and black marketing; (13) Environmental damage.

(1) No freedom — individuals cannot choose their occupations or businesses freely; (2) Abolition of private property kills the incentive to work hard; (3) Lack of profit motive leads to low efficiency and productivity; (4) Bureaucracy and red tape in planning.

(5) Errors in central planning cause shortages and surpluses; (6) Loss of consumer's sovereignty — the state decides what is produced; (7) Dictatorship and suppression of political freedom; (8) Rigidity — difficulty in adjusting to changing needs.

(9) Corruption and favouritism among officials; (10) Denial of religion and moral values; (11) Neglect of quality and innovation; (12) Practical failure — the collapse of the Soviet Union (1991) showed its weaknesses.

(1) Ownership of everything belongs to Allah; man is His trustee, so property must be used according to His commands; (2) Right of private property within limits; (3) Lawful (halal) earning — prohibition of interest (riba), gambling, hoarding, fraud and black marketing.

(4) Zakat, ushr, sadaqat and the law of inheritance for the circulation of wealth; (5) Prohibition of concentration of wealth; (6) Freedom of enterprise with moral limits; (7) Profit-and-loss sharing (mudarabah, musharakah) instead of interest.

(8) Moderation in spending — no extravagance or miserliness; (9) Just distribution and rights of workers — pay wages before the sweat dries; (10) Social security — the state provides basic needs to all; (11) Balance between individual and social interests; (12) Dignity of labour; (13) Fair dealing in trade and honest weights and measures.

Islam forbids the concentration of wealth in a few hands. The Holy Quran says that wealth should not merely circulate among the rich (Al-Hashr 59:7), and warns those who hoard gold and silver (At-Taubah 9:34).

Measures: (1) Zakat and ushr — compulsory transfer from the rich to the poor; (2) Prohibition of interest, which makes the rich richer; (3) Law of inheritance — wealth is divided among many heirs; (4) Prohibition of hoarding, monopoly and speculation; (5) Encouragement of sadaqat and infaq (spending in the way of Allah).

(6) Prohibition of gambling, bribery and unlawful earning; (7) Fair wages to labour; (8) Use of idle land — land not cultivated can be taken back by the state; (9) Responsibility of the state to provide basic needs. In this way wealth keeps circulating, poverty is reduced and society remains balanced.
Ownership: in Islam, Allah is the real owner and man is a trustee; in capitalism, man has absolute ownership of property.
Interest: Islam prohibits interest and uses profit-and-loss sharing; capitalism is based on interest.
Earnings: Islam allows only lawful (halal) earnings and forbids gambling, hoarding and fraud; capitalism allows any profitable activity.
Distribution: Islam ensures circulation of wealth through zakat, ushr and inheritance; capitalism leads to concentration of wealth and inequality.
Freedom: Islam gives economic freedom within moral limits; capitalism gives unlimited freedom (laissez-faire).

Motive and welfare: Islam aims at the pleasure of Allah and social welfare; capitalism aims at maximum profit. Islam provides social security and protects workers' rights; capitalism neglects the poor. Islam keeps a balance between individual and society.
Zakat is a compulsory payment of 2.5% on savings and wealth above the nisab held for one year; it is one of the five pillars of Islam.

Economic importance: (1) Circulation of wealth and prevention of its concentration; (2) Reduction in poverty and income inequality; (3) Discourages hoarding — idle money is invested, increasing production and employment; (4) Raises demand for goods as the poor's purchasing power increases.

(5) Social security for the poor, orphans, widows, disabled and debtors; (6) Reduces the government's welfare burden; (7) Promotes economic stability and growth; (8) Creates brotherhood, cooperation and peace in society, reducing crime and class conflict; (9) Purifies wealth and encourages lawful earning.
